The water lapped at him. The thought floated up unwanted like debris in his mind— they had no reason to keep protecting him if he wasn't of use here. With how often he had hunted them, they would let the current take him back into the dark, and he would deserve it. Distracted by that thought, the third kick missed its mark — his foot sliding wildly off the slick surface and sending him under with a surprised squawk — and the current had him immediately, pulling him sideways through a forest of legs in the dark. A hand caught his wrist, halting his momentum and jolting his shoulder hard enough to hurt, dragging him up and back into the air. He broke the surface sputtering, shaking water from his eyes, and found Dwight — one hand locked around his wrist, the other braced against the alcove wall, breathing hard. Shaking visibly. The ghost of something that wasn't quite a smile on his face, there and gone, the universal language of now we're even. So, they didn’t just let him go after all. Well. Alright then. Leon straightened, shoving his hair back from his face, water streaming off his shoulders. He stared at the planks. Ran the logic again. The wall had flexed. It had made the sound. It should have worked — by any reasonable measure of force applied to material, it should have given at least a little more than it did. “Why didn’t it work? It should have worked. You guys break these all the time!” Danny looked back at him, ribs aching, hip singing from the second impact. “I think... I think She might have fired me. The strength, the cloak... I don't know how long ago. I don't know if I have any of it left." David's expression went through several things in quick succession as he let out a low, venomous snort. That was it. That was the final goddamn straw. “Well, that’s just fucking great.” He pulled Leon aside, fitting himself in the alcove. “Killer wall, no killer strength. Fantastic.” He glared at the boards like they were a personal insult; his shoulder still raw from the back door, lungs burning, chest rattling. “We don’t have TIME for this shit!” He planted his back against the opposite wall, and tilted his chin up from the waterline until he had an inch of air. Looked at the planks. Looked at the ceiling. Took the deepest breath he could manage. Then with a deliberate jump, he drove both legs into the wall with everything he had. The impact hit with a deep, booming crack, felt more than heard, the shock of it traveling up through the floor and into the legs of everyone in the alcove. The planks shuddered — the whole frame shuddered — and the seeping water coming through the gaps turned abruptly to jets, thin hard streams spraying into the dark. David dropped sharply into the dark, water closing over him for one ungraceful second before he found the floor and shoved himself back up, resetting position against the wall and squaring up for another go. “Wait, seriously?” Danny pulled himself higher on Orela’s shoulder, trying to keep his face up. “Do you have any idea how much force it takes to crack that thing??” “You got a better idea?!” He'd broken killer walls. Knew exactly what it took — the particular combination of mass and force and the Entity's gifts behind it, the whole apparatus working together. Without the gifts, the math didn't work. A normal person hitting a killer wall was just a person hitting a very solid wall, and the wall won, and that was the end of it. David hit it again. The sound that came back was wrong. Not the dead thud everything else had made that night — something that carried, that traveled through the water in a pressure wave Danny felt in his teeth. The planks screamed. The whole frame shuddered, the seeping water through the gaps surging to angry jets that sprayed into the dark in thin hard streams. David dropped with the recoil, no support behind him, and was back in position before the current could make a decision about it. The alcove tried to evict him anyway. The surge came from behind, the current finding the narrow space and accelerating through it, and David's footing went sideways. Jake lunged in to catch him, one hand locked around his arm, his uninjured leg wedged against a locker in the corridor like a human doorstop. He was coughing between breaths, the wet rattle of it sitting deep in his lungs, but his grip didn't waver. Leon angled the flashlight. David's face in the beam looked wild. There was no strategy in it, no calculation. All the light could see in his eyes was rage and stubborn determination. He found the wall again with both feet. The boards flexed. Held. But the sound they made on the way back — the long, low groan of wood pushed past what it had agreed to handle — for the first time it sounded like they might actually break. Ch 10 – Suspension The rest of the space between the waterline and the ceiling vanished smoothly. Four feet of it, then three, then two — the ceiling arriving in steady increments as the water found the last of the space and claimed it. They tipped their heads back, chins up, buying seconds. The pipes screamed above them, muffled now, translated by the water into something felt rather than heard. The lockers, the debris, the building's ongoing commentary — all of it reduced to pressure and distant collision, arriving through the water as vibration rather than sound.
